status: Pilot, written by Claude on 12 November 2026, checked by the translation workers, and deployed to earthfluent.com on 13 November 2026. Informal तुम throughout; a male speaker where the verb shows it. The course stores no romanization, so the sound lessons give it in the description.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - A Puff of Breath, Part 1
lessons.description: A puff of breath after a sound makes a different letter, and a different word. Hear pal against phal, and bāt against bhāt.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - Short and Long Vowels, Part 1
lessons.description: Hold a vowel longer and it is a different word. Hear kam against kām, and din against dīn.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - The Line Along the Top, Part 1
lessons.description: Hindi letters hang from a line that runs along the top of each word. Each letter carries a short a of its own unless a mark changes it.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - Vowel Marks, Part 1
lessons.description: A vowel after a letter is written as a mark on that letter. One letter, क, with four marks makes four small words: kā, kī, ke, and ko.

lessons.title: Patterns - To Go in the Present, Part 1
lessons.description: The verb जाना, to go, changes with who is going, and with whether they are male or female. Spot जाता, जाते, and जाती.

lessons.title: Patterns - He Words and She Words, Part 1
lessons.description: Every naming word is a he-word or a she-word, and the verb matches it: जाता for the boy, जाती for the girl.

lessons.title: Patterns - More Than One, Part 1
lessons.description: A word ending in ā changes it to e for more than one: कुत्ता becomes कुत्ते. Others add to the end: किताब becomes किताबें.

lessons.title: Patterns - Words That Match, Part 1
lessons.description: A describing word matches the thing it describes: बड़ा for a he-word, बड़ी for a she-word, बड़े for many.

lessons.title: Sentence Building - The Verb Comes Last, Part 1
lessons.description: English says I eat an apple. Hindi says I apple eat: who, then what, and the verb closes the sentence.

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Asking a Question, Part 1
lessons.description: Put क्या in front of a statement and it becomes a yes-or-no question. Nothing else moves.
words: This is the bus to Delhi.
Is this the bus to Delhi?
क्या यह दिल्ली की बस है?

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Saying No, Part 1
lessons.description: To say something is not so, put नहीं just before the verb.

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Little Words After, Part 1
lessons.description: Where English puts in, on, from, and with in front of a word, Hindi puts them after it: house in, table on.

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Going Places, Part 1
lessons.description: The verb जाना, to go, at work in whole sentences. The place comes before the verb, and the verb comes last.
words: I am going to the market.
We are going to the beach.
हम समुद्र तट जा रहे हैं।
Are you going to the party?
क्या तुम पार्टी में जा रहे हो?

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Questions and Answers, Part 1
lessons.description: A question and its answer, side by side. Hindi says I have as near me there is: मेरे पास ... है.
words: No, I do not speak English.

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Describing Things, Part 1
lessons.description: The thing, then what it is like, then है or हैं to close. The describing word matches: लंबी for the girl, छोटे for the dogs.

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow, Part 1
lessons.description: In Hindi, कल means both yesterday and tomorrow. Only the verb says which: गया था is went, and जाऊँगा is will go.
words: I went to the market yesterday.
I am going to the market today.
मैं आज बाजार जा रहा हूँ।
I will go to the market tomorrow.
